questions.stem: Agrippina the Younger was born in 15 CE at Oppidum Ubiorum, a Roman base on the Rhine. The town is now the city of:
options: Vienna
Marseille
Cologne
London
questions.explanation: Her father Germanicus was commanding on the Rhine at the time. Claudius later made the town a colony named after her, Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium, the origin of the name Cologne.

questions.stem: Under the early principate, imperial women such as Livia held no public office. How could they still exercise power?
options: Through voting in the senate, where women of the imperial family held special seats
Through commanding legions in the provinces when no male relative was old enough
Through the office of consul, which was opened to imperial women by Augustus
Through access to the emperor, patronage, wealth and their role in the succession
questions.explanation: Women could not hold magistracies or vote in the senate, but closeness to the emperor, control of clients and their place as wives and mothers of heirs gave them real influence.

questions.stem: Why did descent from Augustus matter so much for Agrippina and her son?
options: Blood links to Augustus were a key claim to rule in a system with no fixed rule of succession
Roman law said that the throne passed to the eldest living descendant of Augustus through his daughter
Only descendants of Augustus were allowed to enter the senate and hold any public office
The army swore an oath to obey only men whose mothers were related to the Julian family
questions.explanation: The principate had no formal law of succession, so dynastic descent, adoption and the support of the Praetorians and senate decided who ruled. Agrippina was a great-granddaughter of Augustus, and that blood passed to Nero.

questions.stem: Agrippina the Younger's parents were:
options: Claudius and Messalina
Germanicus and Agrippina the Elder
Tiberius and Vipsania Agrippina
Drusus the Younger and Livilla
questions.explanation: Agrippina was the daughter of Germanicus, the popular general, and Agrippina the Elder, a granddaughter of Augustus. Her brother was the future emperor Gaius (Caligula).

questions.stem: Agrippina's mother and two of her older brothers died after falling out with Tiberius and his prefect Sejanus. How might this early experience have shaped her?
options: It left her the sole heir of Tiberius, who adopted her as his daughter in their place
It made her a close friend of Sejanus, who arranged her first marriage as a reward
It showed her how dangerous court politics were and how closely power had to be guarded
It turned her against politics, so she lived quietly on her estates until Nero's death
questions.explanation: Agrippina the Elder and her sons Nero Caesar and Drusus Caesar were exiled or imprisoned and died. Historians often link Agrippina's later ruthlessness to this lesson in survival, though this is an interpretation.

questions.stem: In 28 CE, Tiberius arranged Agrippina's first marriage, to:
options: Marcus Aemilius Lepidus
Lucius Junius Silanus
Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus
Gaius Sallustius Passienus Crispus
questions.explanation: Domitius Ahenobarbus was a nobleman descended from Mark Antony and Octavia. Their son, Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus, born in 37 CE at Antium, became the emperor Nero.

questions.stem: Agrippina's second husband, Passienus Crispus, was a very wealthy former consul who died in about 47 CE. How did this marriage help her?
options: It gave her command of the Praetorian Guard, which Crispus had led for years
It made Nero the adopted son and heir of the emperor Claudius at once
It allowed her to divorce Domitius, who was still alive at the time it took place
It gave her wealth and a respectable position after her return from exile
questions.explanation: Crispus's fortune and status helped Agrippina rebuild her position under Claudius. Domitius had died by 41 CE, and Nero's adoption by Claudius came only in 50 CE.

questions.stem: Early in the reign of her brother Gaius (37-41 CE), Agrippina and her sisters:
options: were sent to live in Egypt as guests of the Ptolemaic royal family
were barred from Rome because Gaius feared their popularity with the army
were honoured on coins and named in public oaths and vows
were made Vestal Virgins and lived in the House of the Vestals
questions.explanation: Gaius gave his sisters extraordinary honours: a coin shows them as personifications such as Concordia, and their names were included in oaths and vows. This was unprecedented for living women.

questions.stem: In 39 CE Agrippina and her sister Livilla were exiled to the Pontine Islands. The charge was that they had:
options: taken part in the murder of Tiberius on the island of Capri
plotted against Gaius with Marcus Lepidus, their sister Drusilla's widower
poisoned their sister Drusilla in order to inherit her vast estates
spoken against Gaius's plan to invade Britain in a letter read out to the senate
questions.explanation: The conspiracy of Lepidus, linked to the general Gaetulicus, was crushed in 39 CE. Agrippina was made to carry Lepidus's ashes back to Rome before being exiled. Claudius recalled her in 41 CE.

questions.stem: Tacitus says that after Messalina's death, Claudius's freedmen each backed a candidate for his new wife. Agrippina was supported by:
options: Narcissus, the freedman in charge of correspondence
Sejanus, the prefect of the Praetorian Guard
Seneca, the philosopher who had been her son's tutor
Pallas, the freedman in charge of the treasury
questions.explanation: Tacitus says Narcissus backed Aelia Paetina, Callistus favoured Lollia Paulina and Pallas supported Agrippina. Sejanus had died in 31 CE, and Seneca was recalled only after the marriage.

questions.stem: Agrippina married her uncle Claudius in 49 CE. What had to happen first?
options: Nero formally renounced any claim to be heir to the imperial throne
The senate changed the law so that a man could marry his brother's daughter
Claudius adopted Agrippina as his daughter and then freed her from his power
The Vestal Virgins declared the marriage blessed by the gods of Rome
questions.explanation: Marriage between uncle and niece counted as incest under Roman law. Lucius Vitellius persuaded the senate to allow marriage with a brother's daughter, clearing the way.

questions.stem: In 50 CE Agrippina received the title Augusta. Why was this significant?
options: It meant she could stand for election as consul
No previous wife of a living emperor had held it
It made her co-ruler of Rome with full legal powers
It was the title given to the commander of the fleet
questions.explanation: Livia became Augusta only after Augustus's death, under the terms of his will. Agrippina received the title while Claudius was alive, a sign of her standing, though it gave no legal powers.

questions.stem: In 50 CE Claudius adopted Agrippina's son, who took the name Nero Claudius Caesar. Why did this matter so much?
options: Nero gained the right to command the legions on the Rhine frontier
Nero, older than Claudius's son Britannicus, became the likely successor
Nero became sole emperor at once, with Claudius as his adviser
Britannicus was formally disinherited by Claudius and exiled from Rome for life
questions.explanation: Nero was about three years older than Britannicus, and his adoption, early coming of age in 51 CE and marriage to Claudius's daughter Octavia in 53 CE made him the leading heir.

questions.stem: Which appointment made in 51 CE, often linked to Agrippina's influence, proved crucial when Claudius died?
options: Pallas as governor of the province of Egypt and its grain
Narcissus as consul and leader of the senate for a year
Vitellius as commander of all the legions in Britain
Afranius Burrus as sole prefect of the Praetorian Guard
questions.explanation: Agrippina had the two prefects, thought loyal to Messalina's memory and Britannicus, replaced by Burrus. In 54 CE Burrus presented Nero to the Praetorians, who hailed him emperor.

questions.stem: Agrippina arranged the recall of the philosopher Seneca from exile in 49 CE. What role did she give him?
options: Commander of the fleet at Misenum, guarding the coast of Campania
High priest of the cult of the deified Augustus in the capital
Tutor to her son, which gave Nero a respected guide and her an ally
Prefect of the city of Rome, in charge of its police and fire service
questions.explanation: Tacitus says Agrippina wanted Seneca, a popular writer, to teach Nero and help plan his rise. Seneca and Burrus later became Nero's chief advisers and, in time, her rivals.

questions.stem: Tacitus says Agrippina had Lollia Paulina, a former rival for Claudius's hand, charged and driven to suicide, and later had Domitia Lepida, Nero's aunt, condemned. What do these accounts suggest about her methods?
options: She was falsely blamed, since both women outlived her by many years
She used her own troops to arrest her enemies in the streets of Rome
She removed rivals through accusations, though Tacitus is a hostile witness
She avoided politics completely and left all such matters to Claudius's freedmen
questions.explanation: Tacitus presents Agrippina destroying any woman who threatened her or her son. The deaths are recorded, but his account of her motives reflects his hostility to women's power.

questions.stem: In 51 CE the captured British leader Caratacus, brought before Claudius, also paid homage to Agrippina, seated on her own tribunal. Tacitus calls this a novelty. What does the episode show?
options: Agrippina was displayed publicly as a partner in imperial power
Agrippina had led the Roman army that defeated Caratacus in Britain
Caratacus was a kinsman of Agrippina through her mother's family
Agrippina had been appointed as governor of Britain by the senate
questions.explanation: Sitting beside the standards to receive a defeated enemy was a role for a commander. Tacitus stresses that no woman had done so before, presenting it as a sign of her unprecedented power.

questions.stem: Claudius died in October 54 CE. Tacitus, Suetonius and Cassius Dio all report that:
options: he was murdered in the senate house by a group of senators
he died in battle against the Parthians on the eastern frontier in Syria
he was killed by the Praetorian Guard during a mutiny over pay
Agrippina was believed to have poisoned him with a dish of mushrooms
questions.explanation: The ancient writers agree on the poisoning story, though they differ on the details. Some modern historians suggest natural causes are possible, since Claudius was elderly and ill.

questions.stem: Agrippina is said to have kept Claudius's death secret until the moment was right to present Nero to the Praetorians. Which conclusion best explains this?
options: The senate had already voted Britannicus emperor and had to be persuaded first
She needed time to secure the guard for Nero before supporters of Britannicus could act
Roman law required a delay of several days before a new emperor could be named
She hoped to rule alone as empress and only changed her mind at the very last moment
questions.explanation: Controlling the timing let Burrus bring Nero before the guard, who hailed him, with the senate then confirming. Britannicus was kept away in the palace.

questions.stem: When Nero became emperor in 54 CE, the first watchword he gave the Praetorian tribune was reported to be:
options: 'the best of mothers'
'liberty restored'
'the gods of Rome'
'the blood of Augustus'
questions.explanation: Tacitus and Suetonius report that Nero gave the watchword optima mater, 'the best of mothers', a public sign of Agrippina's standing at the start of his reign.

questions.stem: A gold coin of 54 CE shows Nero and Agrippina facing each other, with her titles on the main side. Why do historians find this coin so revealing?
options: It was minted in her own name at a mint she controlled in Cologne
No woman had been shown on Roman coinage in such an equal, prominent way
It was issued by the senate to celebrate the end of her influence at court
It proves that she had been formally made co-emperor with Nero by law
questions.explanation: Placing Agrippina face to face with the emperor, with her titles in the more important position, suggests near-partnership. In the next year's issues her image was moved behind Nero's, a sign of change.

questions.stem: Tacitus says that when envoys from Armenia came before Nero, Agrippina began to mount the emperor's platform, and Seneca told Nero to step down and meet her. What does the story show?
options: Nero's advisers acted to stop her appearing to share his public authority
Agrippina had been appointed to lead negotiations with Armenia by the senate
Seneca was trying to hand control of foreign policy to Agrippina herself
The Armenians would only deal with a woman of the Julian royal family
questions.explanation: Seneca avoided a public scandal by having Nero greet his mother before she reached the tribunal. The story marks the start of her loss of influence over Nero's advisers.

questions.stem: Agrippina's influence declined from 55 CE. Which event marked this decline?
options: The senate voted to strip her of the title Augusta and all her property
Pallas was dismissed and she was moved out of the palace with her guard removed
She was exiled to the Pontine Islands for plotting with Britannicus
Nero married her rival Lollia Paulina and made her Augusta in her place
questions.explanation: Nero removed her ally Pallas and, after her threats to support Britannicus, took away her guard and moved her out of the palace. Britannicus was poisoned in early 55 CE.

questions.stem: Tacitus says Agrippina threatened to take Britannicus to the Praetorian camp as the true heir when Nero turned to the freedwoman Acte. Why is this episode significant in Tacitus's narrative?
options: It leads directly to Britannicus's death and shows the conflict in the family
It shows that Agrippina had always preferred Britannicus to her own son
It explains why the Praetorian Guard rebelled against Nero in that year
It proves that Acte was a spy for Agrippina in the imperial household
questions.explanation: Tacitus places the threat just before Britannicus was poisoned at dinner. It shows how the struggle between mother and son had become dangerous for anyone with a claim to rule.

questions.stem: In 59 CE Nero tried to kill Agrippina with a collapsing boat near Baiae. What happened?
options: She escaped to the legions of the Rhine and was killed fighting there
She discovered the plot in advance and poisoned herself before it began
She survived and swam ashore, and Nero then had her killed in her villa
She drowned in the Bay of Naples, and the boat was blamed on a storm
questions.explanation: The plan failed when Agrippina swam to safety. Nero then sent Anicetus, prefect of the fleet at Misenum, who killed her. Nero's letter to the senate claimed she had plotted against him.

questions.stem: Tacitus says Poppaea Sabina urged Nero to kill his mother. Which is the best evaluation of the motives for Agrippina's murder?
options: Agrippina was leading a revolt of the eastern provinces when Nero acted against her
The Praetorians demanded her death in return for supporting Nero as emperor
Nero wished to be free of her control, though ancient writers stress personal causes
Agrippina had been found guilty of treason by the senate in a public trial
questions.explanation: Agrippina opposed Nero's relationships and still had influence and supporters. The ancient sources focus on Poppaea and Nero's character, so historians also weigh the political motive of independence.

questions.stem: After Agrippina's death, Nero's letter to the senate said she had plotted against him. Tacitus says the senator Thrasea Paetus walked out of the senate when thanks were being voted. What does this show?
options: Some senators privately rejected the official story, though few dared protest
The senate had ordered Agrippina's death and was glad that Nero agreed
The whole senate refused to accept Nero's letter and voted against it
Thrasea Paetus had been Agrippina's ally and planned to avenge her
questions.explanation: The senate voted thanks for Nero's escape, and only Thrasea protested by leaving. The episode shows both the senate's compliance and the doubts behind it.

questions.stem: Which was an impact of Agrippina's death on Nero's reign?
options: Nero lost the support of the army and was overthrown that same year
Nero became freer to act as he chose, and his rule grew more erratic
Nero abdicated and handed power to Seneca and Burrus as joint rulers
The empire was divided between Nero and his wife Octavia's family
questions.explanation: Ancient writers see the murder as a turning point: Nero later divorced and killed Octavia and married Poppaea. He ruled until 68 CE.

questions.stem: Which ancient historian gives the fullest account of Agrippina's career?
options: Plutarch, in his Parallel Lives
Caesar, in his Commentaries
Tacitus, in the Annals
Livy, in his History of Rome
questions.explanation: Tacitus's Annals, written early in the second century CE, cover the Julio-Claudians and portray Agrippina at length. Livy and Caesar wrote earlier, and no Plutarch life of Agrippina survives.

questions.stem: Tacitus says he used the memoirs of Agrippina the Younger, which do not survive. Why is this significant?
options: It shows that she wrote her own account of her family's history
It proves that she wrote the official history of Claudius's reign
It means that Tacitus's whole account was copied from her book
It shows that she kept a diary that was later read in the senate
questions.explanation: Tacitus cites her commentarii for a detail about her mother, and Pliny the Elder also used them. It suggests she shaped her own image, though we cannot read her version today.

questions.stem: Tacitus presents Agrippina as ruthless and driven by a desire for power, often unsuited to a woman. A historian evaluating his account should note that:
options: he was Agrippina's freedman and wanted to defend her reputation against Nero
he wrote during her lifetime and could not criticise her openly for fear of death
he never mentions her at all, so his view must be pieced together from coins
he wrote decades later, disliked imperial women's power and drew on hostile sources
questions.explanation: Tacitus wrote under the later emperors Trajan and Hadrian and often uses powerful women to show the corruption of the principate. His facts are generally careful, but his interpretation of motive is coloured.

questions.stem: A relief from the Sebasteion at Aphrodisias, in Asia Minor, shows Agrippina placing a laurel wreath on the head of the young Nero. What does it suggest?
options: The relief was carved after her death to mock her ambition for her son
Agrippina was presented in the provinces as the source of Nero's power
Agrippina had travelled to Aphrodisias and ruled the city as its queen
Nero had been crowned king of Asia in a ceremony performed by his mother
questions.explanation: The relief, from early in Nero's reign, shows her crowning him. Provincial art like this reflects the official image of the dynasty, in which Agrippina was central.

questions.stem: Which is the main value of coins and inscriptions as evidence about Agrippina?
options: They give a full narrative of her life from her birth to her death
They show her official public image, which balances the hostile literary sources
They reveal her private motives, which all of the literary sources leave unclear
They prove that the stories of her crimes in Tacitus were invented
questions.explanation: Coins and inscriptions show how the regime presented her, for example on the coins of 54 and 55 CE. They cannot reveal motives or confirm or disprove particular crimes.

questions.stem: Modern historians such as Anthony Barrett have reassessed Agrippina. Which view is typical of this reassessment?
options: She was a capable political operator in a system that gave women no formal power
She had no real influence and was only a figurehead invented by later historians
She was the true ruler of Rome for twenty years under three emperors
She was innocent of all ambition and wished only to live a private life
questions.explanation: Recent studies treat her as a skilled and ambitious figure who used family, patronage and image to gain power, while recognising that the ancient portrait is shaped by male, senatorial writers.

questions.stem: Which judgement of Agrippina's impact is best supported by the evidence?
options: She ruled the empire alone after Claudius's death until Nero came of age in 59 CE
She had little effect on events, since Claudius chose Nero as heir without her
She secured Nero's succession and briefly held unmatched public prominence for a woman
She changed Roman law so that women could hold the consulship and command armies
questions.explanation: Through her marriage, Nero's adoption and the choice of Burrus and Seneca, she brought her son to power, and early coins show her exceptional status. Nero was already 16 when he became emperor, and he ruled from 54 CE.
